accuracy.evidence: Covers citing textual evidence for explicit and inferred meaning and judging which evidence most strongly supports a claim, as in CCSS RL.7.1 and RL.8.1 and the KS3 English programme ('make inferences and refer to evidence in the text'). The model analysis is sound: 'gripped' and the crumpled pages are physical, involuntary signs of tension in Maya, while 'the hall was packed' is setting and the practice line points to preparation, not nerves. Embedding and trimming advice matches standard secondary English teaching of short embedded quotations.

misconceptions.evidence: Each wrong option is tagged to a named error with its own feedback: evidence about setting rather than the character ('That describes the place, not Leo'), true but off-claim lines, the belief that longer quotations are stronger (trim prediction and the trim check rejecting over-long picks), dropping a full sentence in as a quote (embed step rejects the full-stop fragment), and explanations that retell the quote or merely restate the claim (link step options A and C). The adult text lists the same mistakes, including treating an inference as stated.

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanics specific to quotation work on one original Maya passage: tapping the line that proves each of three claims, dragging quotations into strong/weak/does-not-support bins, tapping first and last word to cut the shortest proving quotation with a live word count, dragging a fragment into a sentence gap so the grammar must still work, and choosing analytical explanations. It deliberately avoids the stated-versus-inferred sort used by flaginfer, and the distinctness gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the rules by acting rather than reading: the packed-hall quote is rejected for the nervous claim and the feedback says why; trimming too much drops the key word 'gripped' and is refused, while trimming too little exceeds the word limit; the full sentence 'Maya gripped her script so hard.' will not fit the gap without breaking the sentence; and only the explanation that zooms in on a verb is accepted as analysis.

predictions.evidence: Three committed predictions before key steps: whether the packed hall or the gripped script is stronger evidence that Maya is nervous, whether a longer quotation is stronger evidence, and whether a good quotation still needs explaining. Each is tested straight away by the step that follows, so a wrong guess such as 'more words give more proof' is overturned by the trim check rather than by being told.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The six-question Challenge (Leo, Sam, a whisper, Tom, Jo, Amir) covers choosing, embedding, explaining, trimming and stated-versus-inferred, and every wrong option carries a misconception tag that gives specific feedback such as 'That describes the place, not Leo. Evidence should show the character.' instead of a bare 'wrong'. The eight-item mastery pool, two parameterised, uses different characters and quotations (Sam's trip, Kai, Zara, Dev, Ellie, Mr Hale) so the quiz does not repeat the Challenge.

readability.evidence: Learner explanation measures FK grade 2.7 against a 6.5 limit and the adult text 5.7 against 9.5, with short sentences and a worked Maya example in every learner paragraph. The lab passage is five short lines, quotations are trimmed to a handful of words, and technical terms (quotation, embed, verb) are used only after they are shown in action, which suits ages 11 to 14.

no_filler.evidence: Every learner paragraph carries one rule with a concrete example from the Maya passage: proof means exact words, strong evidence is about the character and has one reading, short quotes fitted into your own sentence, then zoom in on a word. The content gate found no filler phrases, and the explanation text is under the similarity limit against all other lessons, including the Inferring Characters lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked in a 360 by 640 phone viewport and iPhone 13 and Android screenshots in dark and light themes: word chips wrap onto three rows without clipping, quotation cards and bins are full-width tap targets, drag has tap-and-button alternatives, and the automated phone sweep reported zero findings. The browser gate's Show me run completed on desktop and iPhone 13 within the time limit.

accessibility.evidence: Every interactive canvas element is mirrored by real buttons below it (Line 1 to 5, Strong/Weak/Does not support, every word in the trim step, A/B/C), and the aria-label text reads out the full sentence, the gap as 'blank' and all options. axe passed in both themes in the browser gate, and colour is never the only signal because feedback is also given in words.
